HMRC must get your return and payment by the deadline.

Send a return even if you do not know your profit for the whole year. Check how to send a return without complete profit figures.

The tax year started on 6 April 2025 and ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier returns is finished. You may have to pay a penalty. Send your return or payment soon to avoid more penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to file a tax return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to file a tax return for the previous tax year and you have either:

- never filed a tax return before

- registered before but did not need to file a tax return for the tax year 2024 to 2025

Register with HMRC for Self Assessment to tell them. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email with a different deadline to file your tax return by. This deadline is 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027 or you will get a penalty.

### Sending a paper Return

You can send the Return any time on or after 6 April 2026. You must send the Return. HMRC must receive the Return. HMRC must receive it by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026. If they get it later than this, you will get a late filing penalty.

## Submitting an online tax return

You **must** submit your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you miss this deadline, you **will** get a late filing penalty.

To pay through your tax code, you **must** submit by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026. If you miss this date, you **cannot** use this payment method.

You **can** submit your return any time on or after 6 April 2026 up to the deadline.

### Paying the tax you owe

- If you want to pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027, you must do so or you’ll get a penalty.
- If you make payments towards your bill (known as ‘payments on account’), there is a second payment deadline of 31 July.

**Why estimate your bill?**
You can estimate your Self Assessment tax bill before sending your tax return to:
- give you an idea of what your bill is likely to be
- allow you to budget and pay on time

Find help on understanding the tax you owe.

### Trustees of a registered pension scheme

You cannot send the paper tax return online.

These rules apply if you are a trustee:

*   you can send the paper tax return any time on or after 6 April 2026
*   HMRC must receive the paper tax return by 31 January 2027

### Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

You get more time to submit your return if **both** these conditions are met:

- your partnership’s accounting date falls between 1 February and 5 April
- one of your partners is a limited company

The deadline for your return is:

- **12 months** from the accounting date if you file **online**
- **9 months** from the accounting date if you file on **paper**

### Penalties

If you need to fill in a tax return, you get a penalty if you:

- send your return late
- pay your tax late

You can estimate your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

### If you register late

If you register after 5 October **and** do not pay all of your tax bill by 31 January, you **may** get a ‘failure to notify’ penalty.

The penalty amount is based on the money you still owe. You **will** receive this penalty within 12 months after HMRC receives your Self Assessment tax return.

You can read more about ‘failure to notify’ penalties.

## If you send your tax return late

You will face these late filing penalties:

- an initial £100 penalty
- after 3 months, extra daily penalties of £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900
- after 6 months, a further penalty of 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
- after 12 months, another 5% charge or £300, whichever is greater

To avoid this, send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as possible.

All partners will be charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

### If you pay your tax late

You will pay interest on the amount owed. To avoid this, pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as possible.

You will get a penalty of 5% of the tax you have not paid.

This penalty applies at:

- 30 days
- 6 months
- 12 months

Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

### Your State Pension amount

The amount of money you get in your State Pension is based on your National Insurance record.

You can check this to see:

- how much you might get when you reach State Pension age
- your National Insurance record

The full weekly rate for the new State Pension is £241.30. Your payment might be different if:

- you were contracted out before 2016
- you have a certain number of National Insurance qualifying years
- you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Read more about tax on your retirement income, including what happens if you retire abroad.

## If you get less than £241.30 a week

You may need more qualifying years to increase your State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been contracted out. This meant you paid more into another pension.

If you were contracted out, you usually need more than 35 qualifying years. You need these years to get the full new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

You need 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

### If you get more than £241.30 a week

You get a ‘protected payment’ if:

*   you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016, and
*   you would get more State Pension under the old rules.

They pay this on top of the full rate of new State Pension.

## Annual increases

Your new State Pension goes up by 1% each year. It goes up by the highest of these 3:

- the average percentage growth in wages in Great Britain
- the percentage growth in UK prices (CPI)
- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, it goes up in line with CPI prices.

### Rates

There are two Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |
| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |
| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

### Overpayments and underpayments

You must contact the Child Benefit Office if you receive too much or too little money.

### Benefit cap

Child Benefit counts towards the benefit cap. If the cap affects you, you will still get the full amount of Child Benefit. However, your other benefits may be reduced.

### If families split up

If your family splits up, the money for the eldest child is £27.05 a week.

If you have 2 children and one lives with you while the other lives with someone else (like an ex-partner), you each get £27.05 a week.

If you both claim for the same child, only one of you will get Child Benefit for that child.

If you are entitled to Child Benefit for any other children, you must claim £17.90 a week for each of them.

### If families join together

If your partner also gets Child Benefit, you get £27.05 for the eldest child in the household. You get £17.90 for any younger children.

You and your partner may claim for different children. You cannot both claim at the higher rate if you live together. You may have to pay back some of the money if you do.

You must tell us about the change to your family circumstances.

## If you or your partner earn over the threshold

**The Charge**
*   If either you or your partner’s ‘adjusted net income’ is over the threshold, you may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge.

**Your Adjusted Net Income**
*   Your adjusted net income is your total taxable income before any personal allowances and less things like Gift Aid.
*   Your total taxable income includes interest from savings and dividends.

**How Much You Pay**
*   If you have to pay the charge, the charge will not be more than the amount you get from Child Benefit payments.
*   You can still get the other advantages of Child Benefit like National Insurance credits.

**Work It Out**
*   Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to work out if your adjusted net income is over the threshold.
*   If it is, the calculator will also tell you how much charge you’ll have to pay.

**Who Pays When Both Earn More**
*   If both you and your partner have an individual income that’s over the threshold, then whoever has the higher adjusted net income is responsible for paying the charge.

**If You Earn Much More**
*   If either you or your partner has an individual income of £20,000 or more above the threshold (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you’ll be charged the same amount as you make through Child Benefit payments.
*   You’ll end up with no extra money from Child Benefit.

**Other Options**
*   You can make a claim and opt out of getting payments if you do not want to pay the charge.
*   You can still get the other advantages provided by Child Benefit, like National Insurance credits.

### If you are under 16

You can do both:
* claim for your own child
* let someone responsible for you claim for you

You will usually get more if you claim yourself.

### Universal Credit payments

Universal Credit is paid each month. How much you get depends on:

- your standard allowance
- any extra amounts that apply to you
- any money taken off your payment
- if you’re working, how much you earn

Use a benefits calculator to see how much you could get.

If you get Universal Credit, you’ll earn Class 3 National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension.

### Standard allowance

Your household gets 1 'standard allowance'. Check which applies to you.

| How much you get | Every month |

| If you are single and under 25 | £338.58 |

| If you are single and 25 or over | £424.90 |

| If you live with your partner and you are both under 25 | £528.34 (for you both) |

| If you live with your partner and either of you are 25 or over | £666.97 (for you both) |

## Extra amounts

You may get extra money on your Universal Credit standard allowance. This depends on whether you are eligible.

You must report changes when you become eligible for an extra amount. These amounts are not added automatically. For example, if you become a carer, you must tell DWP. The carer’s element of Universal Credit is not applied automatically if you start getting Carer’s Allowance.

### If you have children

You’ll get £303.94 a month for each child that lives with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you’ll get an extra £47.94 a month for that child.

You get money for each child until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they’re in eligible education or training – for example, they’re studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

### If your child has a disability

You might get an extra monthly amount if any of your children are disabled.

You’ll either get:

- £164.79 - the lower amount

- £514.71 - the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you’re working. If you live with your partner, both of you need to be working, unless one of you is unable to work due to a disability or health condition.

The childcare must be from a registered provider. You can get help paying for childcare including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You need to pay your childcare costs up front. You must claim the money back as part of your payment. You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front. Talk to your work coach after you’ve made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You might get an extra monthly amount if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you’ll get | Extra monthly amount |

| If you have a severe health condition or disability that’s unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |

| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you’ll only get one extra monthly amount. You’ll get the higher amount if one of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you’re moving to Universal Credit, you might also be entitled to a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount known as a ‘carer’s element’. This is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of the following benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

-

Armed Forces Independence Payment 

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

-

Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

-

Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You must provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You’ll get an extra monthly amount of £209.34. If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you’ll only get one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer’s Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work related activity (LCWRA), you cannot also get the carer’s element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it will stop when you claim the carer’s element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs. The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you’re a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken off your payment

If any of these apply, your payments might be reduced:

-
you are paying back an advance on a Universal Credit payment
-
you would get above the amount limited by the benefit cap
-
you’ve been overpaid benefits in the past
-
you owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance
-
you pay your gas or electricity bill directly from your Universal Credit payment
-
you have a paid job
-
you have other income – for example, money from pensions or certain other benefits
-
you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have over £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment will be reduced by £4.35 for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000. Another £4.35 is taken off for any remaining amount that is not a complete £250.

Find out more about money taken off your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that affect how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit at the same time as other benefits. Your Universal Credit payment will be reduced by an amount equal to the other benefit’s payment. This applies when you get Universal Credit and any of the following benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions

- Carer’s Allowance

- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)

- Incapacity Benefit

- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (excluding any increases where constant attendance is needed and for exceptionally severe disablement)

- Maternity Allowance

- Severe Disablement Allowance

- State Pension

- Widowed Mother’s Allowance

- Widowed Parent’s Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)

## Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA.

You might get Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA at the same time. If you do, the amount you get for New Style ESA or JSA reduces your Universal Credit payment.

New Style ESA and JSA are paid more often than Universal Credit.

You also get different National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension. They also may help you get other benefits.

You might get New Style ESA or JSA if your situation changes and your Universal Credit payment reduces or stops. This could happen if:

- your partner earns more money

- you have savings of more than £16,000

Check if you can get:

- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

### Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you apply for Universal Credit, you keep your current benefit for 2 more weeks. You must still be eligible for that benefit.

This applies only if you both get income-related Employment and Support Allowance and Housing Benefit.

You will not pay back extra payments. These payments will not affect your Universal Credit.

If you get a Migration Notice letter, you might also get a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

### Your Universal Credit can be reviewed
- You can have a review
- This makes sure you get the correct money and help
- Read more about Universal Credit reviews
You may get Carer's Allowance. You need to meet certain conditions. This is about you. It is about the person you care for. It is about the type of care you provide.

## The person you care for

To get Carer’s Allowance, you must care for someone who already gets one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component
- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Attendance Allowance
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit
- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate
- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer’s Allowance if you share the care of someone and the other carer is already claiming:

- Carer’s Allowance for that person
- Carer Support Payment for that person
- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit for that person

If you want to get Carer’s Allowance, speak to the other carer about changing their benefits.

If the other carer does not want to do that, you can still apply for Carer’s Allowance. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should receive the benefit.

### The care you give

You must care for someone for at least 35 hours a week. This can include:

- helping with washing and cooking

- taking them to a doctor’s appointment

- helping with home tasks, like managing bills and shopping

### If you get State Pension

1. You **cannot** get the full amount of both Carer’s Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

2. If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer’s Allowance payment.

3. If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you’ll get a Carer’s Allowance payment to make up the difference.

### If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is **more than £86.45 a week**, you **will not** get a Carer’s Allowance payment, but your Pension Credit payments **will** increase instead.

### Pension Credit tops up

This top-up is called ‘Guarantee Credit’.

*   If you are single, your weekly income will go up to £238.
*   If you have a partner, your joint weekly income will go up to £363.25.

You may get extra amounts if you have other responsibilities and costs.

### If you have a severe disability

**If** you get any of the benefits in the list, you **could** get **£86.05** a week extra.

**Either** of these rates counts:
*   the middle rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA), **or**
*   the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)

You can get the extra money **if** you get any of the following:

*   Attendance Allowance
*   the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) at either the middle or highest rate
*   the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
*   Armed Forces Independence Payment
*   the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
*   Pension Age Disability Payment
*   the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance at either the middle or highest rate

## If you care for another adult

You could get £48.15 extra a week if:

- you get Carer’s Allowance

- you get Carer Support Payment

- you’ve claimed Carer’s Allowance but are not paid because another benefit pays more

If both you and your partner have claimed or get Carer’s Allowance, you can both get this extra amount.

## If you’re responsible for children or young people

You can get extra money for each child or young person who lives with you and who you are responsible for.

You will get £69.98 a week for each child.

You will get £81.07 a week for the first child if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You will get this extra money until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday
- 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training - for example, if they are studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

If they are in education, it must be for more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

You can get even more money if the child or young person is disabled.

You can get an extra £37.93 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Child Disability Payment - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component
- Adult Disability Payment - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component

You can get an extra £118.46 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - highest rate of the care component
- Child Disability Payment - highest rate of the care component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - highest rate of the care component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - enhanced rate of the daily living component
- Adult Disability Payment - enhanced rate of the daily living component

You can also get this if they are blind or severely sight impaired.

## If you have housing costs

You might get extra money for housing costs. This includes:

- ground rent if you have a leasehold property
- some service charges
- charges for tents and site rents

The amount depends on your housing costs.

If you get Pension Credit, you may also be eligible for:

- Council Tax Reduction
- Housing Benefit if you rent where you live
- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own where you live

## If you have savings or a second pension

You could get the ‘Savings Credit’ part of Pension Credit if both of the following apply:

- you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016

- you saved money for retirement, for example in a personal or workplace pension

If you are single, you’ll get up to £17.96 a week.

If you have a partner, you’ll get up to £20.10 a week.

You might still get some Savings Credit even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

### Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit you’ll automatically get cold weather payments.

You’ll also be eligible to:

-
apply for a free TV licence if you’re aged 75 or over

-
get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include things such as prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and transport costs for hospital appointments.

## Get help with extra amounts

Contact the Pension Service helpline if you want to know if you can get extra amounts.

Pension Service helpline

Telephone: 0800 99 1234

Relay UK if you cannot hear or speak on the phone: 18001 then 0800 99 1234

British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service if you are on a computer - find out how to use the service on mobile or tablet

Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm (except public holidays)

Find out about call charges

### How long you get SMP for
You can get SMP for up to 39 weeks.

### How much you get
You get:

- 90% of your average weekly earnings (before tax) for the first 6 weeks

- £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower, for the next 33 weeks

### How it is paid
You get SMP in the same way as your wages, for example monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance will be taken out.

### Work out your pay
Use the maternity planner to help work out how much maternity pay you could get.

### If you take Shared Parental Leave
If you take Shared Parental Leave you’ll get Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP). You get £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower.

### Start date

Statutory Maternity Pay usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

It starts automatically if you are off work for a pregnancy-related illness. This must be in the 4 weeks before the week your baby is due.

### Problems and disputes

Ask your employer why your Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP) looks wrong. If you disagree with the amount, or your employer cannot pay (for example, because they’re insolvent), contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team.

### Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) amount and rules

If you are eligible, you can get £123.25 a week or 80% of your normal weekly earnings. You will get whichever amount is lower. It is paid for up to 28 weeks.

You will be paid SSP for all the full days you are off sick. These must be days you would normally have worked.

Your employer will use your average weekly earnings over an 8-week period to work out how much you get. You still qualify if you started your job recently. You qualify even if you have not yet received 8 weeks’ pay. Ask your employer to find out more.

## How you’re paid

Your employer pays SSP. They pay it the same way they pay your normal wages. This could be weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, you may get SSP from each employer.

Tax and National Insurance will be taken out.

If you think you’re not getting the right amount of SSP, talk to your employer. If you’re still not happy, contact the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

### Your age and job

Your minimum wage depends on your age. It also depends on whether you are an apprentice.

You must be:

- at least school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage
- aged 21 to get the National Living Wage

The minimum wage still applies to workers aged 20 and under.

## Current rates

Rates change every 1 April.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |
| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

Apprentices get the apprentice rate if they are either:

- under 19
- 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship gets £8 an hour.

Apprentices get the minimum wage for their age if they have both:

- aged 19 or over
- finished the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 who has finished the first year of their apprenticeship gets £12.71 an hour.

### Who gets the minimum wage

Read who has a right to the minimum wage.

Use the minimum wage calculator to check if you get the National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage.

Contact Acas if you do not get the National Minimum Wage and think you should.

### Your letter
*   You will get a letter in October or November saying how much Winter Fuel Payment you can get.
*   You only get this if you are eligible.
*   You do not need a letter to know you are eligible.
*   If you do not get a letter, check if you must claim.

### How the amount is worked out
The amount you get depends on:
*   when you were born
*   your circumstances between 21 and 27 September 2026

This period is called the ‘qualifying week’.

### Other benefits
Any money you get will not change your other benefits.

## If your income is over £35,000

You have earned more than £35,000.

HMRC must take back your Winter Fuel Payment.

They will do either one of these things:

- change your tax code
- add the amount to your Self Assessment tax return

You can check if your total income is more than £35,000 and how HMRC will take it back.

### If you live alone or no one with you qualifies for the Winter Fuel Payment

You will get either:

### What Marriage Allowance Does

Marriage Allowance lets you give £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the amount you can earn without paying tax.

This lowers their tax by up to £252 in the tax year (6 April to 5 April the following year).

You can also read this guide in Welsh (Cymraeg).

### Who Can Claim

To gain from this, you (the lower earner) must normally have income below your Personal Allowance. This allowance is usually £12,570.

### How to Calculate Your Savings

You can calculate how much tax your couple could save. You should call the Income Tax helpline if:

*   you receive other income such as dividends, savings or benefits from your job; or
*   you do not know what your taxable income is.

### How It Affects Tax

When you transfer some of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner, you might have to pay more tax yourself. But your couple could still pay less in total.

### Example

Your income is £11,500. Your Personal Allowance is £12,570, so you do not pay tax.

Your partner’s income is £20,000. Their Personal Allowance is £12,570, so they pay tax on £7,430 (this is their 'taxable income'). As a couple, you are paying Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance, you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310. Your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

This means you will now pay tax on £190. But your partner will only pay tax on £6,170.

As a couple, you benefit. You are only paying Income Tax on £6,360 rather than £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic or intermediate rate, which usually means their income is between £12,571 and £43,662.

These things will not stop your application:

*   you or your partner currently receive a pension
*   you or your partner live abroad - as long as you get a Personal Allowance

### Who can get statutory redundancy pay?

You normally get statutory redundancy pay if you are an employee.

### How much pay will you get?

You get:

-   half a week’s pay for each full year you were under 22
-   one week’s pay for each full year you were 22 or older, but under 41
-   one and half week’s pay for each full year you were 41 or older

Your length of service is capped at 20 years.

### How is weekly pay calculated?

Your weekly pay is the average amount you earned per week.
It is based on the 12 weeks before the day you got your redundancy notice.

If you were ‘on furlough’ because of coronavirus and paid less than usual, your pay is calculated differently.
It is based on what you would have earned normally.

### What are the limits?

If you were made redundant on or after 6 April 2026:
-   Your weekly pay is capped at £751.
-   The maximum statutory redundancy pay you can get is £22,530.

You have 6 months from the date your job ends to apply for statutory redundancy pay.

## Exceptions

You cannot get statutory redundancy pay if:

- your employer offers to keep you on
- your employer offers you suitable alternative work and you refuse without good reason

Dismissal for misconduct is not redundancy. You cannot get statutory redundancy pay if this happens.

You cannot get statutory redundancy pay if you fall into one or more of these categories:

- former registered dock workers (covered by other arrangements) or share fishermen
- crown servants, members of the armed forces or police services

You can claim statutory redundancy pay. You must be eligible. You must also have been temporarily laid off. This means you had no pay or less than half your weekly pay. This must be for one of these reasons:

*   more than 4 weeks in a row
*   more than 6 weeks that do not come one after the other in a 13 week period

Tell your employer in writing that you want to claim statutory redundancy pay. You must do this within 4 weeks of your last day without work in the 4 or 6 week period.

If your employer does not reject your claim within 7 days of getting it, tell them again in writing. Give them your notice.

Your employer can reject your claim if your normal work is likely to start within 4 weeks. Your work must also continue for at least 13 weeks.

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

If you’re a basic rate taxpayer, the rate you pay on gains from 6 April 2026 depends on your gain and taxable income.

You can see the rates and allowance for earlier years.

To work out your rate:

- Work out your taxable income. Subtract your Personal Allowance and other Income Tax reliefs from your income.
- Work out your total taxable gains.
- Subtract your tax-free allowance from your total taxable gains.
- Add the result to your taxable income.
- If this total is within the basic Income Tax band, you’ll pay 18% on gains made from 6 April 2026.
- You’ll pay 24% on gains above the basic Income Tax band made from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (income minus Personal Allowance and Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000. Your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, subtract the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your gain. The allowance is £3,000 for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. This leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The total is £29,600. This is less than £37,700 (the basic rate band for 2026 to 2027). You pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

You’ll pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (income minus Personal Allowance and Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000. Your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, subtract the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your gain. The allowance is £3,000 for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. This leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The total is £69,600. This is more than £37,700 (the basic rate band for 2026 to 2027). You will pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700 and 24% on £31,900.

You will pay £10,842.

### What it is

Inheritance Tax is a tax on the estate of someone who has died. An estate is made up of their property, money and possessions.

### When you do not pay

There is normally no Inheritance Tax to pay if either:

- the value of your estate is below the £325,000 threshold

- you leave everything above the £325,000 threshold to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club

You may still need to report the estate’s value even if it is below the threshold.

### When the threshold can change

If you give your home to your children (including adopted, foster or stepchildren) or grandchildren, your threshold can increase to £500,000.

If you are married or in a civil partnership and your estate is worth less than your threshold, any unused threshold can be added to your partner’s threshold when you die.

### Other languages

## Inheritance Tax rates

The rate is 40%. You only pay this on the part of your estate above the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000. Your tax-free threshold is £325,000. You pay 40% on £175,000. This is £500,000 minus £325,000.

If you leave 10% or more of the ‘net value’ to charity in your will, you can pay a lower rate of 36% on some assets. The net value is the estate’s total value minus any debts.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you make while alive may be taxed after you die. Depending on when you gave the gift, ‘taper relief’ might mean you pay less than 40% tax on it.

Other reliefs, such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, let you pass on some assets with no tax or a lower bill.

### Who pays the tax to HMRC

The tax comes from money in your estate.
The person who manages the estate pays this to HMRC.
This person is called the ‘executor’ if you have a will.

Your beneficiaries usually do not pay tax on what they inherit.
They may pay related taxes in other cases.
For example, they may pay tax on rental income from a house left to them in a will.

People you give gifts to might have to pay Inheritance Tax.
This only happens if you give away more than £325,000 and die within 7 years.

### What’s a premium, deductible, coinsurance, or copayment?

### Premiums

**Monthly Premium**

*   $0 for most people. You qualify if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 10 years.
*   You won’t pay a Part A premium if you get Medicare earlier than age 65.
*   If you aren't eligible for $0 part A premiums, you may buy Medicare part A
*   If you buy Part A, you’ll pay either $311 or $565 each month. Your cost depends on how long you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes.
*   You must sign up for Part B to buy Part A.
*   If you don’t buy Part A when you’re first eligible for Medicare (usually when you turn 65), you might pay a penalty.

### Deductible

**Each benefit period**

*   $1,736 for each inpatient hospital benefit period, before Original Medicare starts to pay.
*   You pay the Part A deductible each time you start a new benefit period.
*   There’s no limit to the number of benefit periods you can have in a year.
*   This means you may pay the deductible more than once in a year.

### Inpatient Stay

**Daily Costs**

During a benefit period, what you pay depends on how long you get care:

*   **Days 1-60:** $0 each day after you pay your Part A deductible.
*   **Days 61-90:** $434 each day.
*   **Days 91-150:** $868 each day while using your 60 lifetime reserve days.
*   **After day 150:** You pay all costs.

### Skilled Nursing Facility Status

**Daily Costs**

During a benefit period, what you pay depends on how long you get care:

*   **Days 1-20:** $0 each day after you pay the Part A deductible.
*   **Days 21-100:** $217 each day.
*   **Days 101 and beyond:** You pay all costs.
*   You don’t have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period.

### Home Health Care

*   $0 for covered home health care services.
*   20% of the Medicare-approved amount for durable medical equipment (like wheelchairs, walkers, hospital beds, and other equipment).

### Hospice Care

*   $0 for covered hospice care services.
*   A copayment of up to $5 for each prescription drug and other similar products for pain relief and symptom control while you're at home.
*   5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care.

### Out-of-pocket limit

**Yearly**

*   There’s no yearly limit on what you pay out-of-pocket.
*   This rule does not apply unless you have supplemental coverage, like a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy or join a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C).

### Sign Up Early

You must sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. This is true unless you have other coverage that is similar in value to Medicare (like from an employer). If you do not sign up, you may pay extra money. This is called a late enrollment penalty.

### Late Enrollment Penalties

These penalties:

- Are added to your monthly premium.
- Are not a one-time late fee.
- Are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage (for most people, that’s a lifetime penalty). The Part A penalty is different.
- Go up the longer you wait to sign up. They are based on how long you go without coverage similar to Medicare. Find out when you should sign up to avoid penalties.

### Part A late enrollment penalty

*   You must buy Part A if you do not qualify for free Part A.
    [Do I qualify for free Part A?]()
*   If you must buy Part A, and you do not buy it when you are first eligible, your monthly premium may go up 10%.
*   You must pay the penalty for twice the number of years you did not sign up.

**Example:**
If you were eligible for Part A for 2 years but did not sign up, you must pay the higher premium for 4 years.

Usually, you do not have to pay a penalty if you meet certain conditions that allow you to sign up for Part A during a Special Enrollment Period.

[Find out if you are eligible for a Special Enrollment Period.]()

### Part B late enrollment penalty

You usually do **must** not pay a Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. You also do **cannot** pay the penalty if you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program. Learn more about Special Enrollment Periods.

You **will** pay an extra 10% for each year you could have signed up for Part B, but didn’t.

You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.

### Example:

If you waited 2 full years (24 months) to sign up for Part B and didn’t qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you **will** have to pay a 20% late enrollment penalty. This is 10% for each full 12-month period that you could have signed up. You **must** also pay the standard Part B monthly premium ($202.90 in 2026). 

### 2026 Calculation:

$202.90 (2026 Part B standard premium) 
+ $40.58 (20% [of $202.90] late enrollment penalty)

$243.48

$243.50 will be your Part B monthly premium for 2026. This amount ($243.48) rounds to the nearest $.10. It includes the late enrollment penalty.

### Part D late enrollment penalty conditions

- You will not pay a penalty if **both** of the following are true:
  - You have creditable drug coverage (coverage about as good as Part D) **OR**
  - You qualify for Extra Help

- You **will** pay an extra 1% for each month (12% a year) if **both** of the following are true:
  - You **did not** join a Medicare drug plan when you first got Medicare.
  - You **went** 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage.

- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.
- The plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty after you join. It will also tell you what your premium will be.

### If you do not agree with the penalty

Example:
If you waited 14 months to join after you were eligible, and you **did not** have creditable drug coverage, you **will** pay a 14% penalty. You add this to your monthly plan premium.

- The penalty amount comes from the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026).
- The national base beneficiary premium changes each year. Your penalty amount may change each year.
- This penalty is added for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage. It stays even if you switch plans.

In 2026:

$38.99 (2026 national base beneficiary premium)
X   0.14 (14% penalty)

$5.46 (rounded to the nearest $0.10 = $5.50)
$5.50 **will be** your monthly penalty for 2026. Add this amount to your plan’s monthly premium.

## Do I need to sign up for Medicare when I turn 65?

You can answer questions to find out when you should sign up. You can also review the scenarios below to find out when you should sign up.

### If you (or your spouse) have health insurance from a job:

If you or your spouse are still working, you may be able to wait to sign up for Medicare. If you wait and sign up later, you will not pay a late enrollment penalty. This applies where you have group health insurance that is available to everyone at the company.

- If you don’t have to pay a premium for Part A (Hospital Insurance), you can choose to sign up when you turn 65 (or anytime later).
- You can wait until you (or your spouse) stop working to sign up for Part B (Medical Insurance). You can also wait until you or your spouse lose your health insurance, if that happens first. You will not pay a late enrollment penalty.
- Once you stop working (or lose your health insurance, if that happens first) you have an 8-month Special Enrollment Period (SEP) when you can sign up for Medicare. You can also add Part B to existing Part A coverage. The SEP starts when you stop working (or lose insurance), even if you choose COBRA or other coverage that’s not Medicare.

Ask the employer that provides your health insurance if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. If you don’t sign up for Part A and Part B, your job-based insurance might not cover the costs for services you get.

Where you’re self-employed or have health insurance that’s not available to everyone at the company (like retiree coverage):

Ask your insurance provider if your coverage is employer group health plan coverage (as defined by the IRS). If it’s not, sign up for Medicare when you turn 65. If you do not sign up, you will pay a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty.

If you have retiree coverage from a previous job, it may not pay for your health services if you don't have both Medicare Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance). Ask your benefits administrator how your retiree coverage works with Medicare.

Don’t risk losing your retiree coverage — check before joining a plan.

The employer may offer coverage when you have Medicare, like a supplemental plan, drug coverage, or Medicare Advantage Plan. If they do, ask if you or your family will lose your retiree coverage if you join a plan the employer doesn’t offer.

### If you have health insurance that’s not from a job:

Answer questions to find out when to sign up for Medicare. You will get other important information based on the specific type of coverage you have. The rules vary depending on what type of other health insurance you have. Contact your health insurance plan to get more information. This applies to insurance from Medicaid, Marketplace, or another private company.

If the insurance is like insurance you bought with a stipend from work:

Ask your health insurance company if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. Some private insurance companies have rules that lower what they pay (or don’t pay at all) for services you get if you’re eligible for other coverage, like Medicare. Once you sign up, Medicare pays first.

### If you have COBRA coverage:

If your job offered you COcobra coverage after your employment ended:

The rules may vary. Contacts your health insurance plan to get more information. This applies if you have not signed up for Medicare yet.

- Sign up for Medicare when you turn 65. If you do not, you will have gaps in coverage and will pay a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty.
- Your COBRA coverage will probably end once you sign up.

Don’t wait until your COBRA coverage ends to sign up for Part B. COBRA coverage does not extend your limited time to sign up for Medicare.

This applies if you got COBRA after you signed up for Medicare:

COBRA pays after Medicare (unless you have End-Stage Renal Disease).

### If you don’t have health insurance:

Your coverage start date depends on two things:

## Your first chance to sign up (Initial Enrollment Period)

Generally, this period starts when you turn 65. This is called your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months in total. It starts 3 months before you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.

Avoid the penalty
If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up. You may also have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage. You may also have to pay a penalty if you have to pay a Part A premium, also called “Premium-Part A.” Learn more about how to avoid late enrollment penalties.

### Premium

Your total cost for Medicare drug coverage depends on the plan you choose. Depending on the plan, you may pay:

**Premium:** A monthly amount you pay for coverage, whether or not you get drugs.

- Your premium depends on the plan you choose.
- You may have to pay more if you have a high income.
- Who pays a higher Part D premium because of income?
- If you have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty, it will be added to your monthly premium.

**Tip:** Even if you don’t take many drugs now, or your out-of-pocket drug costs are low, consider getting a drug plan with a low monthly premium. This can help you avoid the late enrollment penalty. All plans must cover a wide range of drugs that people with Medicare take.

### Other Costs You Might Pay

- **Deductible:** An amount you pay for covered drugs and items each year, before your plan starts to pay. Your deductible depends on the plan you choose. No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $700 in 2027 ($615 in 2026). Some plans have no deductible.
- **Copayment:** A fixed amount you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.
- **Coinsurance:** A percentage you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.

### Medicare drug coverage stages

Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage Plans with drug coverage usually have 3 stages:

- **Deductible stage:** If your Medicare plan has a deductible, you must pay all costs yourself until you reach the full amount. No Medicare drug plan can have a deductible more than $615 in 2026 ($700 in 2027). Some Medicare drug plans do not have a deductible.
- **Initial coverage stage:** After you reach your full deductible (if your plan has one), you must pay 25% of the cost for generic and brand-name drugs. You pay this until your out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027). This total includes certain payments made for you, like through the Extra Help program. Then, you will automatically get "catastrophic coverage."
- **Catastrophic coverage stage:** You will not have to pay costs for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

When you have Medicare drug coverage, you should get an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) the month after your plan bills the pharmacy. Your EOB shows the prescriptions you filled, what your plan paid, what you and others paid, your coverage stage, and what counts toward your out-of-pocket costs and your total drug costs.

### How do I pay my plan’s premium?

You can pay your premium in these ways:

- Your plan deducts the cost from your checking or savings account.
- You charge it to a credit or debit card (fees may apply).
- Your plan sends you a bill each month. Some plans bill for next month’s coverage in advance. Send your payment to the plan, not to Medicare. Ask your plan for their payment address.
- Your plan withholds the cost from your Social Security payment. Ask your plan, not Social Security, for this option. It may take up to 3 months to start.

If premiums were not withheld from your Social Security payment until 1 or 2 months after you joined a Medicare drug plan, you will get a bill for those months. You must pay your drug plan’s monthly premium directly to your plan for those months. Your plan will tell you when the withholding from your Social Security payment is set up.

### How can I lower my drug costs

Some programs can lower your drug costs if you qualify.

*   **Medicaid**: This program helps cover medical costs for some people with limited income and resources. It is funded by the federal government and each state. Each state has different rules about income and resources to decide who is eligible. Contact your state to see if you are eligible.
*   **Extra Help**: This Medicare program helps pay your drug costs. You automatically qualify for Extra Help if you qualify for Medicaid, one of the Medicare Savings Programs, or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits from Social Security. If you do not automatically qualify for Extra Help, you can apply.
*   **Medicare’s Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET)**: This Medicare program gives temporary Medicare Part D drug coverage. You must qualify for Extra Help or Medicaid but not yet be enrolled in a Medicare drug plan. LI NET covers all Part D covered drugs. There are no network pharmacy restrictions.
*   **State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (SPAP)**: These programs help pay your drug plan premiums and/or cost sharing. They are provided by your state or the U.S. Virgin Islands. SPAP contributions may count toward your Medicare drug coverage out-of-pocket limit. Eligibility depends on each program’s specific rules.
*   **Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (PAPs)**: Some drug companies offer programs to help pay for medications for people in Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Look for a Pharmaceutical Assistance Program (PAP) for your drugs to lower prescription costs. Each company has different eligibility rules to participate in their program. Contact the company to see if you are eligible and start getting help.

The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is a new payment option. It works with your current Medicare drug coverage. It helps you manage your out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by your plan by spreading them across the calendar year (January–December). This payment option might help you manage your monthly expenses, but it does not save you money or lower your drug costs.

## What’s the Part D late enrollment penalty?

This penalty is money that is permanently added to your Medicare Part D premium.

You may owe this penalty if you go 63 days or more in a row without either:

*   Medicare drug coverage, or
*   Other creditable prescription drug coverage.

This applies after your Initial Enrollment Period is over.

After you join a plan, the plan will tell you:

*   If you must pay a penalty.
*   What your premium will be.

You generally must pay the penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

### How much is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The plan calculates the penalty by multiplying:

*   1%
*   times the “national base beneficiary premium” ($38.99 in 2026)
*   times the number of full, uncovered months.

You were eligible to join Medicare drug coverage during those months, but you didn’t. You also didn’t have other creditable prescription drug coverage.

The amount is rounded to the nearest $.10. It is added to your monthly premium.

The “national base beneficiary premium” may go up each year. Your penalty amount may also go up each year.

**Example:**

If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a plan, and you didn’t have creditable drug coverage, you must pay a 14% late enrollment penalty. This is in addition to your monthly plan premium.

The penalty is added to your premium for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage. This applies even if you switch plans.

However, if you get Extra Help, you **don’t** pay a late enrollment penalty.

A court order gives you appeal rights. You have these rights if the hospital changes you from "inpatient" to "outpatient". You must also meet other rules.

You can ask for an appeal if you meet both rules below:
*   The hospital admitted you as an inpatient on or after January 1, 2009.
*   The hospital changed your status to “outpatient getting observation services”.

You can ask for a fast appeal if both rules below are true:

You can ask for this while you still have to stay in the hospital. Learn how to file this type of appeal.

### Why does hospital status matter?

Your hospital status changes how much you pay. It also changes how Medicare covers you. Medicare may or may not cover care at a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after you leave the hospital.
